messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The record DOI/URL matches the source DOI and URL exactly (10.1002/aws2.1269, https://doi.org/10.1002/aws2.1269).

The source supports that the study used full-scale GAC adsorbers in Minnesota operated in a lead–lag configuration ("Full-scale adsorbers in MN were operated in a lead–lag configuration"), but it does not explicitly state that this was a "municipal groundwater treatment facility" even though that is a reasonable inference. Core elements (full-scale, MN, lead–lag) are supported.

The source states that PFAA removal from GW and SW was studied with two sub-bituminous coal-based GACs and that full- and pilot-scale adsorbers contained as-received GAC with 12×40 US mesh particle size operated in packed-bed lead–lag configuration, matching the description of packed-bed GAC adsorbers using as-received sub-bituminous coal-based 12×40 mesh GAC.

The source describes PFAA removal from groundwater (GW) in MN and indicates TOC = 0.7 mg/L for GW. Together with the methods describing full-scale adsorbers in MN, this supports the description of Minnesota groundwater used for drinking water treatment with TOC 0.7 mg/L.

The abstract and methods describe perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAAs) and specifically mention seven PFCAs and three PFSAs in breakthrough curve data, supporting the description of PFAAs including PFCAs and PFSAs and multiple chain lengths.

The paper repeatedly discusses PFAA removal and breakthrough curves (bed volumes to 10% and 50% breakthrough), which is a removal-type performance endpoint. The chosen endpoint_type of "removal" is consistent with this.

The source states that within PFCA and PFSA subclasses, adsorbability increased with chain length as evidenced by more bed volumes treated to onset/10%/50% breakthrough (Table 1) and that consistent differences in PFAA adsorption capacity were not observed for EBCTs of 13 and 26 min in full-scale GW adsorbers. These statements support the interpretation regarding chain-length-dependent adsorbability and lack of consistent EBCT effects on carbon use rates.

The term summarizes the study focus on PFAA breakthrough and adsorbability in full-scale GAC adsorbers, which is consistent with the described full-scale breakthrough curves and bed volumes to 10%/50% breakthrough.

The limitation is marked design_inferred and notes specificity to one groundwater utility, one GAC type/particle size, and EBCT range 13–26 min. The source confirms a single full-scale MN GW system, as-received 12×40 mesh GAC, and EBCTs of 13 and 26 min. It is reasonable to infer limited generalizability from these design facts.

The source explicitly states that in GW no consistent effect of EBCT (13 and 26 min) on carbon use rates was observed, and that consistent differences in adsorption capacity were not observed for EBCTs of 13 and 26 min. However, it does not explicitly frame this as complicating scale-up based solely on EBCT or attribute it to DOM characteristics or pore blockage in this specific context. Those aspects are interpretive extensions, so the limitation is only partially supported.
The methods describe as-received GAC with a 12×40 US mesh particle size and a 0.92 mm logarithmic mean diameter for full- and pilot-scale adsorbers, matching the recorded value string.
The field is treated as descriptive text for particle size (mesh and mm) and leaves unit null; this is consistent with the mixed descriptor reported in the source.
The source states a hydraulic loading rate of "~12 m/h" for the full-scale adsorbers. Recording 12 with a qualifier indicating it is approximate matches this information.
The hydraulic loading rate is reported in the source as m/h and the unit is correctly captured as m/h.
The methods report EBCTs of 13 min for each full-scale vessel. The recorded value of 13 is correct.
EBCT is expressed in minutes in the source, and the unit is correctly given as min.
The source explicitly states that full-scale adsorbers in MN were operated in a lead–lag configuration, consistent with the description of lead–lag GAC adsorber vessels operated in series.
Configuration is a descriptive field and correctly has no unit.

The methods note that full-scale adsorbers were operated for a period of 4.8 years, and that data presented are from start-up to reconfiguration at 23 months, matching the stated operational period and qualifier.
The operation duration is given in years in the source, and the unit years is appropriate.
The methods report that GAC in the lead vessel was replaced 23 months after start-up, matching the recorded value.
The replacement time is in months in the source, and the unit months is correctly recorded.
The source notes that samples were collected monthly from October 2006 to June 2011; encoding this as a sampling frequency of 1 per month is consistent.
Sampling frequency is correctly expressed as per month, consistent with monthly sampling in the source.
The abstract/methods state TOC for MN GW as 0.7 mg/L, matching the recorded value.
TOC is reported in mg/L in the source and the unit mg/L is correct.
The paper indicates that EBCTs of 13 and 26 min were used and that no consistent effect on carbon use rates was observed. The value "13 and 26" correctly lists the EBCTs being compared.
EBCT values are in minutes in the source, and the unit min is appropriate.
The methods report that full-scale adsorbers in MN were operated for 4.8 years. The value 4.8 (years) is correctly transcribed as an exact numeric.
The duration is expressed in years in the source, and the unit years is correct.
The source states that GAC in the lead vessel was replaced 23 months after start-up. The value 23 is correctly captured as exact_numeric.
The replacement time is given in months, and the unit months is appropriate.
The methods state a hydraulic loading rate of "~12 m/h". Recording the value as "~12" with value_form approximate_numeric matches the source.
Hydraulic loading rate is in m/h in the source, and the unit m/h is correctly recorded.
The EBCTs for each full-scale vessel are reported as 13 min in the methods. The value 13 is correctly captured.
EBCT is in minutes in the source, and the unit min is correct.
The TOC of MN groundwater is reported as 0.7 mg/L in the abstract/methods. The value 0.7 is correctly transcribed.
TOC is expressed in mg/L in the source, and the unit mg/L is appropriate.
The source states that no consistent effect of EBCT (13 and 26 min) on carbon use rates in GW was observed. Representing the EBCT range as 13–26 min is consistent with the reported EBCTs.
The EBCT values being compared are in minutes; the unit min is correct.

The abstract notes that the volume of SW that could be treated to 10% or 50% PFAA breakthrough was about 50–60% of the GW volume under the given comparison. The range 50–60 is correctly captured as a percentage.
The throughput comparison is expressed as a percentage (50–60%); the unit % is appropriate.

The study directly compares PD-RSSCT, pilot-scale, and full-scale GAC adsorbers using the same GAC type and particle size, examining bed volumes to 10% and 50% breakthrough and scale-up factors between MN GW full-scale and NC SW pilot-scale systems. Inferring that these configurations are comparable with conditions aligns with the described design and scale-up analysis.

The explanation that comparability is based on shared GAC type, similar operating concepts (EBCT, breakthrough-based performance), and specific GW matrix/DOM conditions is consistent with the methods and results describing full-scale MN GW, pilot-scale NC SW, and PD-RSSCT comparisons, including TOC values and bed volumes to 10%/50% breakthrough.

result.record_usable_rationale: All core elements—study identity, matrix (MN groundwater), treatment configuration (full-scale lead–lag packed-bed GAC with defined particle size and EBCT), PFAS scope (PFAAs including PFCAs and PFSAs), and quantitative operating and performance descriptors—are directly supported by the cited source text. The only partial support concerns an interpretive limitation statement, which does not affect the core quantitative findings or endpoint definitions. The record is therefore usable for synthesis of scale-up and comparability of GAC adsorption performance.
